title: Ornamental Plant Production infrastructure, equipment and technology

lessons.title: Nursery structures and growing areas
lessons.html:
Where plants are grown

A nursery is laid out in areas that match the stages of plant growth. Each area has its own structure and conditions. Knowing what each structure does helps the supervisor use it properly and spot problems early.

Main structures

StructureMain use
Propagation house (mist or fog)Rooting cuttings and germinating seed in high humidity
Greenhouse or tunnelGrowing tender plants protected from cold, rain and wind
Shade houseGrowing shade plants and hardening young plants; shade net reduces light
Open beds or blocksGrowing on hardy shrubs and trees in full sun
Potting shedMixing media, filling containers and potting under cover
Dispatch areaPreparing, grading and loading orders

Shade net and coverings

Shade net comes in different densities, for example 30%, 40% or 80% shade. Plants such as ferns and clivias need heavy shade, while most flowering shrubs need little or none. Tunnel plastic ages in the sun and lets through less light over time, so it must be checked and replaced when worn. Torn net and plastic should be reported and repaired before wind makes the damage worse.

Ground and drainage

Growing areas are often covered with weed mat, gravel or concrete. A good surface drains well, stops weeds and keeps pots clean. Standing water breeds disease and mosquitoes and makes paths slippery. Check that drains and slopes are working after heavy rain.

Layout and access

Paths must be wide enough for trolleys and, where needed, a tractor or bakkie. Blocks should be labelled so that workers and pickers can find stock quickly. A logical layout reduces walking and handling, which saves time and damage.

lessons.title: Irrigation, climate control and nursery equipment
lessons.html:
Keeping conditions right

Irrigation systems

  • Overhead sprinklers water blocks of small pots evenly but waste some water between pots.
  • Drip irrigation delivers water to each large container through drippers or spaghetti tubes.
  • Mist and fog systems keep cuttings moist with very fine droplets, usually on a timer or a leaf sensor.
  • Hand watering with a hose and rose is used for small batches and dry spots.
  • Fertigation injects liquid fertiliser into the irrigation water through a dosing unit.

Water comes from boreholes, dams or municipal supply. Under the National Water Act 36 of 1998 water use may need to be registered or licensed, so follow the nursery's water rules and report leaks at once. Filters must be cleaned regularly; blocked filters and drippers are a common cause of dry plants.

Climate control

Greenhouses may have fans, roof or side vents, wet walls, heaters and thermostats. Some nurseries use bottom heat (heated benches or cables) in propagation to speed rooting. Check thermometers and humidity readings daily and record them.

Equipment

  • Potting machines and media mixers
  • Tray fillers and seeders
  • Trolleys, Danish trolleys and pallet jacks
  • Knapsack sprayers and motorised sprayers
  • Secateurs, knives and hedge trimmers
  • Tractors and trailers on larger nurseries

Safe use and maintenance

Only trained and authorised workers may operate machines. Guards must stay in place, and machines must be switched off and isolated before cleaning or clearing a blockage. Never put hands into a running mixer or potting machine. Keep tools sharp and clean; disinfect cutting tools between batches to stop disease spreading. Report faults immediately and do not use broken equipment. Wear the protective equipment required for each task, such as gloves, dust masks when mixing media, and the chemical-resistant clothing listed on spray labels.

lessons.title: Technology in modern nurseries
lessons.html:
Using technology to grow better plants

Technology helps nurseries produce more plants of better quality with less water, labour and waste. Even small nurseries now use some of these tools.

Automation and controllers

Irrigation controllers switch zones on and off at set times. More advanced systems use sensors for soil moisture, temperature, humidity and light, and can open vents or start fans automatically. The supervisor still needs to check plants in person, because a sensor can fail or be placed in the wrong spot.

Measuring tools

  • pH and EC meters test irrigation water and the growing medium. EC (electrical conductivity) shows how much fertiliser salt is present. Readings outside the nursery's target range must be reported.
  • Thermometers and data loggers record temperature over day and night.
  • Scales weigh fertiliser and media ingredients accurately.

Record and stock systems

Many nurseries use computer programs or phone apps to record batches, stock, sprays, orders and labour. Barcodes or QR codes on labels allow quick stock counts and order picking. Accurate data capture by the supervisor is essential: a system is only as good as the information put in.

Container and media technology

Plug trays, air-pruning containers, biodegradable pots and controlled-release fertilisers all improve root quality and reduce labour. Recycled and reusable containers reduce waste.

Looking after infrastructure

A simple maintenance plan keeps everything working: daily checks of irrigation and climate, weekly cleaning of filters and benches, monthly checks of structures, nets and electrical equipment by a qualified person, and immediate reporting of faults.

Key points

  • Each structure, from mist house to open blocks, suits a different growth stage.
  • Clean filters and drippers prevent dry plants; report water leaks.
  • Only trained workers use machines, with guards on and power isolated before cleaning.
  • Sensors and controllers help but never replace checking plants in person.
  • pH and EC meters help keep water and feeding within target ranges.
